headline: A multi-signer S/MIME envelope validates every signer's certificate chain, and a primitive that names one of its error codes names them all
summary: `b.mail.crypto.smime.verifyAll` verifies every SignerInfo's signature but validated only the first signer's certificate chain, then returned `chainVerified: true` for the whole envelope. A second signer whose certificate chained to nothing the caller supplied was accepted. It now validates every signer's chain. `b.tsa.verifyToken` reads one SignerInfo, and RFC 3161 allows a timestamp token the TSA's signature and no other, so a token carrying a second signature is refused rather than judged on its first. Alongside that, 34 primitives documented some of the error codes they throw and not the rest, which left operators writing a catch for a list that was never complete; the omitted codes are documented and a gate holds the lists complete from here.

items.title: verifyAll validates the certificate chain of every signer, not the first
items.body: `b.mail.crypto.smime.verifyAll` is the multi-signer entry point: it verifies each SignerInfo against its own key in `signerPublicKeys` and reports `valid: true` only when every one verified. When `trustAnchorCertsPem` was supplied it validated one chain, the first signer's, and returned `chainVerified: true` as a property of the envelope. So a two-signer message whose second certificate chained to no supplied anchor passed `valid && chainVerified`, which is the check an operator writes. Every signer's chain is validated now, and the first failure refuses the envelope. A single-signer envelope and a multi-signer envelope whose signers all anchor behave as before.

items.title: A chain check is bound to the certificate its SignerInfo names
items.body: Validating each signer's chain was not enough on its own: the chain walk picked its leaf by matching the public key that verified the signature, and took the first certificate in the bundle that matched. Two SignerInfos naming different certificates that carry the same key therefore validated the same chain twice, so an envelope holding one anchored certificate followed by an unanchored one with the same key returned `chainVerified: true` with the second certificate never walked. A SignerInfo's sid names its certificate by issuer and serial together, and that pair now picks the certificate whose chain is walked. Matching the serial alone would not do: a serial is unique only within an issuer (RFC 5280 section 4.1.2.2), so a bundle may legitimately hold two certificates with one key and one serial under different issuers, and the sid says which is meant. When no certificate in the bundle both carries the verifying key and is the one the sid names, the envelope is refused with `mail-crypto/smime/signer-cert-not-named`, because a chain validated for any other certificate describes an identity the SignerInfo never claimed. A sid that identifies its certificate by subject-key identifier instead names no issuer and serial, so it cannot be bound to a bundle entry at all: chain validation refuses it with `mail-crypto/smime/unbindable-sid`, and verifying that envelope without `trustAnchorCertsPem` is unaffected.

items.title: A timestamp token carrying a second signature is refused
items.body: RFC 3161 §2.4.2 gives a time-stamp token the TSA's signature and no other. `b.tsa.verifyToken` reads one SignerInfo, so a token carrying two was verified on the first and accepted, leaving the second read by nothing. Such a token now raises `tsa/multiple-signers`. A token with no SignerInfo still raises `tsa/no-signer`, and a conformant single-signer token is unaffected.

items.title: b.x509Chain.canonicalNameKey compares two distinguished names as names
items.body: `b.x509Chain.canonicalNameKey(nameNode)` returns one comparable string for an X.501 `Name`, the shape a certificate's issuer and subject fields carry, normalized per RFC 5280 section 7.1. Two encodings of one name, in `PrintableString` or `UTF8String`, in either case, or with repeated inner spaces, give the same key, and attribute order inside a single relative distinguished name does not change it. An empty `RDNSequence` keys like any other name, since RFC 5280 section 4.1.2.6 permits an empty subject when the identity is in `subjectAltName`. A structure that only resembles a name returns `null`: every node is checked for its tag, its class and whether it is constructed, so a relative distinguished name written as a `SEQUENCE`, one holding no attribute, an attribute that is not exactly a primitive object identifier and one value, or a value whose tag number matches a string type under another class refuses rather than keying, each of which would otherwise key the same as the well-formed encoding. A value that does not read as text keys by its bytes together with its full tag identity. Two `null`s are not a match, so check for `null` before comparing. The S/MIME chain check uses it to decide which certificate a SignerInfo names.

items.title: Primitives that document an error code document all of them
items.body: An error code is what an operator writes in a catch, and 34 primitives named some of theirs and left the rest undiscoverable. `b.csp.build` named one of nine, so `csp/header-injection`, `csp/unsafe-keyword`, `csp/catch-all-source` and `csp/data-source` reached nobody. `b.mail.crypto.smime.checkCert` attributed the SHA-1 and short-RSA refusals to `mail-crypto/smime/bad-cert` when they arrive as `mail-crypto/smime/refused-hash` and `mail-crypto/smime/rsa-too-small`. `b.problemDetails.create` named one of eight, `b.guardManageSieveCommand.validate` one of eight, and the `parseNotification` method on the handle `b.auth.ciba.client.create` returns one of seven. Others wrote their list as a run of bare suffixes after one full code, so `b.safeDns.parseResponse`, `b.safeIcal.parse`, `b.safeIcap.parse` and `b.safeVcard.parse` listed sixteen, sixteen, eleven and twelve codes with only the first of each written in full, which no operator can search for. Each code is now written out with the condition that raises it. `b.guardMarkdown.render` named one of four and omitted the size-budget refusals, `b.fileType.assertOneOf` named one of five and called a second `EMPTY`, which is not a code the framework raises, and `b.auditSign.rotateSigningKey` named one of three. No behavior changed in any of these.

items.title: guardImapCommand describes the per-verb checks it performs
items.body: `b.guardImapCommand`'s documentation described a per-verb argument-shape check refusing with `guard-imap-command/bad-shape`. No such check and no such code exist. What the verb selects is which caps run: a zero-argument verb refuses arguments with `guard-imap-command/unexpected-args`, a mailbox-first verb has the name measured against the mailbox cap, a sequence-set-first verb has its element count measured, and a SEARCH-family verb has its parenthesis nesting measured. Argument arity beyond the zero-argument verbs is not checked, which the documentation now says, so a listener that needs `LOGIN` to carry exactly two arguments checks that itself.

items.title: S/MIME trust anchors are documented on the primitives that read them
items.body: `trustAnchorCertsPem` turns on certificate-chain validation in `b.mail.crypto.smime.verify` and `b.mail.crypto.smime.verifyAll`, and appeared only in the namespace's prose, so an operator reading either primitive could not find how to enable it. Both now document it, including that omitting it verifies the signature and leaves the chain unchecked. `b.mail.crypto.smime.checkCert` documents `certPem`, which until now appeared only inside its example.

items.title: Two envelopes that used to verify now refuse
items.body: A multi-signer S/MIME envelope passed to `b.mail.crypto.smime.verifyAll` with `trustAnchorCertsPem` refuses when any signer's certificate does not chain to a supplied anchor, including the case where two signers name different certificates carrying the same key. A bundle whose certificates carry the signer's key but do not include the one the sid names raises `mail-crypto/smime/signer-cert-not-named` from both `verify` and `verifyAll`, and an envelope whose sid is a subject-key identifier raises `mail-crypto/smime/unbindable-sid` when trust anchors are supplied; verifying it without anchors is unchanged. If one of these starts refusing, the envelope was being accepted on one signer's chain: supply the anchors for every signer, or verify the signer you care about through `b.mail.crypto.smime.verify` with that signer's key. A timestamp token carrying more than one SignerInfo raises `tsa/multiple-signers` from `b.tsa.verifyToken`; a conformant RFC 3161 token carries one and is unaffected.

items.title: A block that names an error code must name every code its function throws
items.body: `test/layer-0-primitives/operator-doc-error-codes.test.js` reads each documented primitive's error codes out of its comment block and compares them against the codes its function constructs. A block that names none is out of scope, since it documents nothing to be partial about. So is a block above a function that opens a further function, because a code constructed inside a nested function is thrown when that function runs, from a returned handle or a listener, rather than by the primitive the block describes; the gate reports how many blocks that boundary holds back so the scope cannot quietly shrink. It runs in the static-gate block, in about a second, rather than inside smoke.
